utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom, also to those who are technically assisting us; the interpreters and the technical staff. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed cross-examining the witness Mr. Ashton as soon as he has been brought in this courtroom, unless there's any other thing to be raised by the parties. Yes, there's one thing. Mr. Usher, would you please wait for a moment. Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. May I remind you, Ms. Pilipovic, that you almost took a time similar, already, to the Prosecution in cross-examining the witness; and I think that it was more or less a guideline of the Trial Chamber in its earlier decision, which was not quashed on appeal, that you should not take any more time than the Prosecution in examination-in-chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to my calculations and records, the Defence has -- the examination-in-chief lasted seven hours and 50 minutes. I think that the Defence has used up, according to my own calculations, five and a half hours, which gives us a little leeway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... seven hours and 50 minutes is not correct, but we'll come to that a little later, at the first break. I think it was approximately six and a half hours, and you're almost at six and a half hours, so would you please -- could you give us an estimate on how much time you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best and complete my cross-examination by the first break, which means one to one-and-a-half hours more, of course with the Court's indulgence and permission, if we agree that the time that the Prosecution has taken is more and is approximately equal to our own calculations. Let me stress that there were quite a few technical problems during the cross-examination, which took up quite a lot of time, and as the Defence is not able to have access to the transcript on the day in which the proceedings end -- for example, I got the transcript late last night of last week, of the 14th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to urge you to see whether you can do it in one more hour, and we'll come to that in far more detail on a Status Conference, which will be held - and I'm addressing myself also to the Prosecution at this moment - at the very end of tomorrow morning's session. That means after the last break, we'll have a Status Conference, and I ask the parties already to prepare, especially the Prosecution at this moment, since they're presenting their case, to give it some consideration as to how to speed up the presentation of the case. But we'll do that tomorrow for the last three quarters of an hour. You may proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th of January, 2002, we left off while discussing the map that you were looking at, and I should like the usher to present the witness with that map now. I think the number of the map was 344.A. It is the map the witness marked in the positions asked of him. Witness, I asked you to mark in the apartment blocks behind the line which you said and designated as the positions of the army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You visited those lines? You told us you did.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me how often you went to that part of town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Grbavica about once every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you said you talked to the soldiers, do you happen to know whether there was any water and electricity in that part of town, from what you learnt from them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They never -- they had water and electricity when I was there. Also, they had gas when the other side of the city didn't have natural gas. But there were sporadic outages. That much I know from talking to the pharmacist in Grbavica when I went to see her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked to the soldiers who were up at the front lines there, in talking to them, did you hear whether they were locals from that part of town where the lines were? Did they live there too? Were their homes in the vicinity? Were they locals?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few of the soldiers I spoke to lived in Grbavica before the conflict. A few more of them had come from across the front line, from downtown Sarajevo over to Grbavica, or from the surrounding areas right near the city. Most of the people were, yes, generally from that area, from Sarajevo. In fact, I don't recall talking to anyone that was not from Sarajevo down in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to know any of them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three or -- three of them that I know that would always come up to me when I drove into the area and greet me. It was one of them that took me on a little tour of the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that, at the lines there, they were defending their own homes and their households, in view of the fact that they were locals and lived there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask for me to agree with that, no, I can't agree with that because the problem was the opposing forces were actually the ones defending themselves. The amount of ammunition and weaponry I saw in Republika Srpska on that front line was quite extensive as opposed to what the Bosnians claim they had, and since I didn't go to that Bosnian front line on that side, I don't know, but I know that several assaults were made, while I was there, by the Republika Srpska towards the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you didn't go around the Bosnian positions. How can you say that they were poorly armed, then, if you didn't visit them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I didn't visit them directly opposing that position; however, I did go to Trg Heroje Bosnian front lines in July, and again in October, November of 1992, and in 1993, and the Bosnians never had enough weapons. They traded the weapons when they left the front lines. They were given ten rounds to twenty rounds of ammunition each. And that was what I was told was all the way around. And when I went to Dobrinja and I went down to the Stup front line, it was all the same; the Bosnians had very little material, purely defensive. They were told not to fire unless they were told to fire or they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- you first said that you didn't visit the Bosnian army positions and now from your answer I understand that you did go to Hrasno and Dobrinja and Stup, the positions there. Could you tell us about Dobrinja; which were the positions of the BH army there? And do you happen to know what unit, military unit, military formations, was in Dobrinja itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Dobrinja and Stup, all of us working for the United Nations or journalists, everyone had to go through the front lines to get to the airport. The airport road ran through there and the road later constructed by the UN at the end of the runway towards Lukavica from Dobrinja was running through the front line so you had contact every day with those areas. Now, I never did visit the actual line along the Dobrinja front on the -- going across the airport road. I was not allowed into that area; just where the crossings were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mark Dobrinja on the map for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you draw a circle around Dobrinja, please, and the road, route you took to the airport.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, just to let you know, I'm not going to indicate -- this line on the front side is not going to indicate the exact front line. This is just the area of Dobrinja, as you requested, okay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that circle, is that where Dobrinja is, the Dobrinja settlement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you -- could you tell us what route you took from town to reach Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. From town -- and I'll draw the route for you, I'll mark the route. Actually, it was this here. This was the corner I would turn. And then the last Bosnian checkpoint was here, front line, and then at the airport perimeter there was a French checkpoint, and this here was considered No Man's Land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the hospital in that part, the hospital you visited?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was somewhere in this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you go to Dobrinja, to the hospital there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the hospital, I only went five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers in Dobrinja, armed and uniformed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that was the front line.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: A few moments ago, Ms. Pilipovic made an observation to the witness that he had earlier said that he had not visited Bosnian army positions, and now -- and she made a comment to the effect that he was now contradicting himself. She made that observation, then went on to ask him a question. Since then, I've been checking the transcript. I've found the reference; page 1558. Indeed, that's not what the witness said. He specifically said that he did visit positions. I rise to my feet at this stage simply to request, Mr. President, that in future, when Ms. Pilipovic puts to the witness what he has earlier said and suggests that he has contradicted himself, that, in fairness, she also put to the witness exactly what it was that she thinks he said earlier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, there might be some misunderstanding, as far as I understood the question and the answer given by the witness. I noticed that Ms. Pilipovic asked the witness whether he -- how he would know about the BiH weaponry, and then he answered that he was told that there was not very much. And then he said he didn't visit -- but I think he said he didn't visit it on that side, which of course doesn't mean that he did not visit one of the other sides where BiH army might have been. But let's not pay too much attention to it. I do agree with you that exact quoting is of major importance in order to avoid any misunderstanding. At the same time, I'd like to ask Ms. Pilipovic, since Dobrinja has not been part of the examination-in-chief, what exactly is her case as far as Dobrinja is concerned at this moment? Because that's what is required for touching upon ground in cross-examination if it's not touched upon by the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said that he visited the hospital in Dobrinja, and the reason I asked -- what I asked him was how -- was how he got to Dobrinja, to mark the route he took, and how you get to Dobrinja, to the hospital, and I think he has confirmed what he said, and that was why I asked him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked to the soldiers, Witness, at those positions, the ones you marked in, did you meet an officer on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't ever recall meeting an officer. That doesn't mean there might not have been one present, but I never recall having met one or seen one there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people you talked to, do you know which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I only know that they identified themselves as the defence corps for that neighbourhood, that community. One of them always referred to himself as a member of the defence unit, local defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you marked in the facilities behind the front line held by the BH army forces, you marked in the Marsal Tito barracks and its location. Do you happen to know how many barracks there are in the city of Sarajevo, were in the city of Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 29th and 30th of October and 1st of November, 2001, on page 03041485, you said, and you're talking about the area and district of the Holiday Inn and Presidency, you said that in that area there were no significant BH army facilities that I knew about except the front line towards Vasin Han, and that the Serbs targeted the Bosnian positions from their own positions -- had they targeted, they could have hit the bases easily and the concentrated forces of the BH army, like the Austro-Hungarian fortress and the Sedrenik area in the eastern part of town. When you said that, what positions of the BH army did you have in mind? What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fortress, which I never went into but I was told that was a Bosnian army-held position, and also the Tito barracks, the two buildings in Tito barracks, I never saw those buildings targeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand what you're saying, you say that the building like an Austro-Hungarian fortress, was under the control of the army -- the Bosnian army, as you yourself say.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told; I didn't go in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that previously it had been the Jajce barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall hearing that expression, no, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, were you informed that the Viktor Bubanj barracks existed and that it was in fact a prison, there was a prison in it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. I was not informed of that. I don't even know where that's located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said you were in Dobrinja, what you have just stated, that is to say, your comments to your statement, you said that in the eastern part of town, the BH army troops were concentrated. Can you mark in the positions of the BH army in that part of town for us now, please, on the map. Could you mark that in? Because you said the Austro-Hungarian fort was pointed out to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never visited the eastern front lines the entire time I was there, and I don't know of any, as you used the term, concentrations of forces. I knew they were stretched very thin around the lines throughout Bosnia, but I never heard about any concentration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just read out to you what you yourself stated and you confirmed and said that you abide by everything that you stated in your statements. At this point, I should like to show you a map -- a photograph, that is; 306. I made enough copies for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you intend to tender this photograph into evidence, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It would be D22.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the photograph that you yourself took?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the picture that you took at the moment you were up on the roof of the Holiday Inn hotel? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to the roof of the Holiday Inn; that was much too dangerous. I was up on the 10th floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was from the 10th floor that you were able to observe this incident and take the picture?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I moved from the 10th to the 6th floor, up and down, during the shelling, during this particular shelling incident. For safety reasons, I moved up and down and out of the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that you had seen when the -- the moment when the shell exploded.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's been put to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's been put to the witness that he testified that he had seen the moment when the shell exploded. In fact, he has not testified to that effect. However, in an annexure to his statement signed on the 1st of November, he has referred to this incident. I'd be grateful if my friend could make the distinction between testimony and what the witness has said in his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic, it would --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In annex 2 of the statement, the witness speaks about the photograph 306 on page 2 of the annex, under number 10, and he says as follows: "I saw when the shell fell near the car which was racing down the street," and I asked him whether he saw the shell explode or fall down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness confirm that he stated that he saw the shell explode -- that he saw the shell fall down next to the car which was speeding down the street? Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the shell explode next to the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please point to us on the photograph the spot where the shell exploded.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on the photograph, ma'am. The car was moving very fast down the sniper's alley there. He was going at a high rate of speed. The shell landed right in front of the museum. He ended up in front of the next building past the museum, going west on the road. He travelled quite some distance after the car was hit and ended up in that spot there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us how it was that you failed to film the location where the shell exploded, though you stated that you had seen the shell explode?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have pictures of where that shell exploded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have pictures of the location where the shell left traces or a picture showing the shell fall down and explode?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have a picture of a shell exploding moments before, in the same location, before that car arrived. I also photographed the area where the shell was being fired from, and at a later point that day, as the attack carried on into the evening and darkness arrived, you could see the muzzle flash on the hill above the cemetery. Every time the mortar fired, then there was a pause, and then the mortar would explode down in front of the Holiday Inn, in front of the museum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see at that moment the position from which the shell had come?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I could not see the people there, but I could see the flash of the outgoing mortar when it was fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a shell or a mine?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mortar round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from the Holiday Inn hotel was the location where the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No more than 60 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what side of the Holiday Inn hotel did you take the photograph of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facing Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you then explain your statement that the shell had come from the top of Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question, because -- unless you're asking me which side of the Holiday Inn Trebevic is on, and that's the same side as Trebevic that faces Grbavica. You can see Grbavica from that side of the Holiday Inn and you can see Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you are referring to the statement of the witness, could you please quote him literally, because the Chamber has not available these statements. So would you please then always literally state the statement of the then prospective witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, sir, please explain to me what locations were you able to see, what position were you able to see from the spot where you were standing, from which you took the picture? What positions were you able to observe from the place where you were at the time you took photographs of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to view a very wide panorama from as far down -- above the sports stadium in Grbavica to the furthest point on Trebevic, where it went around and you couldn't see any further back in the valley that went back the other direction. The only obstacle in the way was the former, I guess it was parliament building that stood across from the Holiday Inn. That blocked some view, but a very small segment of the view, of Bistrik, the Jewish cemetery area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Grbavica stadium?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you were staying at the Holiday Inn hotel, did you have any knowledge as to the fact that the headquarters of the BH army were located at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the lobby every day with the journalists, where we had our briefings. We never saw anyone except an occasional soldier come in to talk to the hotel manager. But we never saw any soldiers in the Holiday Inn, just on a very rare occasion when they would pass through to talk to the manager or talk to a journalist who was going to do an interview. That's the only time I ever saw soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those occasions when you interviewed soldiers or where some other journalists interviewed soldiers, did you also take photographs of such interviews, in particular, the interviews with members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not take any photographs of the soldiers there because they were not of interest to my media coverage. However, I do want to make a comment here. If you use the term "soldiers," there were United Nations French and Canadian soldiers that came into the Holiday Inn and out of the Holiday Inn on a regular basis, to check on us. The Canadians had a food contingent there and I saw them every day, come and go. So that's just to clarify the fact that there were soldiers, in the terminology of "soldiers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about the soldiers of the BH army and whether you saw them and whether you knew that the Main Staff of the BH army was located there, and you told me you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please respond once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My friend has just made an observation that this witness has said he didn't know whether the Main Staff of the Bosnian army was located in the Holiday Inn. That is incorrect. The witness was asked whether he had any knowledge as to the fact that the headquarters of the army were located at the hotel. That appears at line 10 of page 14. He said, effect, he had no knowledge. That cannot be interpreted as a denial -- as him saying that he didn't know whether they were located there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I think, literally speaking, you're right, if you say, "I didn't know," that leaves open that it might have been there but you were just not aware. But the answer of the witness went a bit further, saying that he had no reasons to believe that it was there because he never saw any soldiers. I think this was quite well understood by this Chamber, and I think these are minor issues that will not be unnoticed by the Chamber itself and take a lot of time. So if it's not really touching upon the essence of the statement -- of course, you're always free to object whenever you want, but let's try to find some discipline for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will -- I hear what you say. My concern was that when one reads this transcript at a later point, undue weight might be given to these observations which are in the transcript, but I understand what Your Honour is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me that question, and I want to tell you that I had access to every room in the hotel. I was able to go up, because the lobby is an open atrium and you see everybody coming and going in and out of the hotel. There were only three entrances in use in the hotel all during the time I was there and during the time I visited. I also spent time down in the Canadian section, talking to the Canadians, in the basement where they were keeping their food for UNPROFOR. The kitchens, the conference room and the entire front area facing Grbavica where the conflict zone was, there was absolutely no soldiers in there of the BiH, in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me complete my question. While you were staying at the Holiday Inn hotel, did you at any point in time ever see a soldier of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you see them there and how many would they be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, only one at a time, once a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us, please, what kind of uniform they were wearing, if they were wearing uniforms. But because they were soldiers, I presume that they were in uniform. So what kind of uniform did they have and what kind of insignia did they have on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing both camouflage and solid green uniform on those soldiers. At one time I remember one sitting, talking to one of the camera crews from CNN or CBS or ABC - I don't know which crew it was - and he had a Bosnian symbol on his shoulder, the shield with the fleurs-de-lis, and he had a hat with the same symbol on it, a beret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see BH army soldiers wearing any other type of uniform except for the one that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I saw the camouflage uniforms and the green uniforms. I just -- I wasn't paying much attention to their uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also see those soldiers in town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not those specific soldiers, but occasionally I'd see soldiers, yes. Every now and then one would pass me in the street, but the soldiers were not armed in town that I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to those soldiers when you saw them? Were you in their vicinity, since you're saying that they were not armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a couple of occasions, I was stopped by two soldiers or three soldiers standing together, just to ask who I was, check my identity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 14, 15 of the transcript of the 11th of January, 2002, in response to a question put to you by my colleague Mr. Blaxill, you said that you had contact with the civilian protection organisation, and the interpretation was on a daily basis, every day. Would you please explain to us what the civilian protection is and on what basis you had this daily contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used to go up to the skating rink in Sarajevo, underground, where all the food was kept. The United Nations convoys would come in, and I met quite a few of the civilian protection people there who were in charge of distribution of food. When I was down in Hrasno district, I was approached by civilian protection many times. I knew a few of the people there, who warned me that I was not supposed to go any further or the military would stop me in a certain area along the line if I wasn't escorted. For the most part, all I knew is they were involved in the food distribution, and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed, those people, people from the civil protection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those I saw were dressed in civilian clothes most of the time. There were some dressed in blue overalls. At one time the government had gotten some German street-cleaning uniforms. They were like coveralls, winter coveralls, warm coveralls, sort of a pinkish colour. Some of the people complained to me about the colour, saying it was so bright that it was easy for snipers to shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you had noticed them at various checkpoints in town.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were police checkpoints around the town to check everybody's ID papers, and there was always one or two civilian protection there at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can therefore agree that, while in town, you would see people in uniform, in police uniforms, uniforms of the civil protection organisation, and olive-drab uniforms, also people wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, did you become aware of Juka Prazina, Caco? Did you ever hear about these individuals from your colleagues and did you have contact with those people, Bajromovic as well, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I encountered Juka once in an incident at the State Hospital. I knew about him. I did not see them very often. I knew that other journalists had interviewed them, but I knew they were around, because I heard a lot of stories about them from the local people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From those people, did you ever hear about the fact that they had their own military formations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also hear from them that those paramilitary formations terrorised the civilian population in town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, I would like to show you a picture. It's the picture number 2391272 and 273. Actually, two photographs. That would be Defence Exhibit D23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whilst the photograph is distributed, Ms. Pilipovic, I'd like to inform you that the Prosecution took six hours, 45 minutes for examination-in-chief, and that you took, until now, approximately seven hours. So I would draw your attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember these photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the other photograph, ma'am? Because I have two of the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes. I provided both photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since these are two different pieces of paper, would you please renumber them such that both of them have a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last two digits, 1272, 1273.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two of the exact same photographs here. I don't have the numbers on the photographs, but there are two different photographs in that correspondence, she is right, but one of these is the wrong photograph that I'm holding.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask that the originals be shown to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to have them marked?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- So that he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They look very much like the photographs we had in the bundle. Do you want them to be marked by the witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The originals are marked 1272 and 1273, if the witness could confirm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please tell us when it was that you took the first of these photographs that we're now looking at.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was about 9.30, 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what part of the bus were you at that point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the very front, near the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on that bus while you were inside of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came around a turn and we turned parallel towards Grbavica. I marked that on an earlier map, as a matter of fact, when we discussed this incident. The bullet came down through the window on the right side of the bus, and angled down towards the bottom underneath the windows on the left side of the bus. The French UNPROFOR determined that it had been fired from above the area of the sports stadium in Grbavica. They checked the bus and they checked the angle of the trajectory of the bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the spot where the bullet struck, and did the glass break?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please show us on the photograph the place where the glass was broken.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near the back of the bus, in here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please explain to us how it was that you did not take a picture of the exact spot in the bus where the glass was broken.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the bus stopped and everybody got off and ran for cover, including myself. I didn't -- the bus was still out in view of the sniper position. I didn't want to go back into the bus. In fact, I went straight to the UNHCR office, which was only a few blocks away, and reported it, and asked for the French, if they could come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the second photograph now, 1273, please, the original that you have in front of you. Could you explain why these people in the bus are laughing? Why is that man standing up there smiling, as far as I'm able to see?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a scream from one woman. I recall her yelling out and I heard people saying things under their breath in anger. I don't know if that's laughter or if that's an expression of excruciation or anger. I don't know. There were some people who just stood there, even when the bullet came through, they didn't even bother to more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, did the shot hit the window, the glass, and was it shattered at the moment they all crouched down? Why were they -- why did they react in this way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we all heard the crash, we -- I jolted, and I saw the people go down. One gentleman who was on the bus, standing next to me, said to me afterwards, before I had left the scene - who spoke English - he said that, "It doesn't matter if you duck, because the bullets go right through it anyway."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take the photograph of the bus with the shattered glass after that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. The French did, though. They have it in their archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I have one more question for this witness, and that would conclude my cross-examination, and I would be respecting the time set by you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, while you were in Sarajevo, you said that you had contacts with the HVO soldiers, and you said that you had contact with soldiers who were members of the army of the Bosnian Serbs and that you would see soldiers belonging to the BH army. Will you agree with me when I say that if those people used weapons, and if during the time that you spent in Sarajevo they used those weapons, were all the people living in that region traumatised and afraid? Did they all suffer from trauma and fear?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, for a variety of reasons, they did suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're standing up. What would you like to inform the Court about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I simply took note of the fact that the Prosecution was very specific about semantics. Quite simply, the witness said something. I don't think it was what he meant to say. He stated that literally a mortar round exploded, in French, [French phrase], but we -- to specify, Mr. President, it was on page 12, line 22. What I'm reading in English, and I quote, for Mr. Ierace: "[In English] Down in front of the Holiday Inn." And Mr. Ierace will correct me if I'm wrong, was the shell. [In English] But I'm not quite sure of that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this create any further misunderstanding or would this -- could this cause any confusion? If not, I'd just like to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From my perspective, Mr. President, it doesn't cause any confusion at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the court is not confused by it either, so thank you very much for your observation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The Defence has concluded the cross-examination of Mr. Ashton. Is there any need of re-examination? Mr. Blaxill, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, indeed, we do have about four or five points and I hate to say we guarantee, but I almost guarantee we should conclude before the break. Re-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, firstly I would like to ask you this: My learned friend suggested to you had you ever heard Galic give orders about, I think it was the iron cross. My question is this: Did you at any time see or hear General Galic give or appear to give orders to anybody or about anything?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I see him directly give orders?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- a little later, you made reference in a question about sniper rounds of 7.62 millimetres to a maximum range of 1.000 metres. By that, sir, what exactly did you mean? Did you mean that was the maximum effective accurate range or the maximum distance a bullet could physically travel of such a calibre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a bullet can travel way longer than that from that calibre. That was the maximum effective range with a very good marksman, which there were plenty around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few minutes ago, Mr. Ashton, you were referring to the incident with the motor car that was in the picture that my learned friend put to you. You identified the source of fire. Can you say what happened to the occupant or occupants of that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in that -- in this explanation, I will explain something that was just brought up. When I refer to mortar round, I refer to a mortar shell. When I refer to an artillery round, I refer to an artillery shell. The mortar round - mortar shell, for clarification - landed next to that vehicle. The vehicle went out of control, crashed into the tracks. There was a woman in the passenger side of the vehicle and there was a man in the car, and he desperately tried to get her out, and another shell landed back towards the museum, directly in front of the Holiday Inn, and he ran to a building across the street, scrambled underneath sort of a little basement overhang there. I have a picture of that. He hid there for some time as the shells continued into the dark. He could not get out of that position. I later learned that the woman was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any idea of the age of the person, the lady?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: She seemed to be a young woman, but I wasn't close enough, actually, to -- there was a lot of smoke in the car too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- and can you confirm the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was around July 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You also referred, in the course of cross-examination, to an incident on the 14th of July. By that I refer to the incident near the Holiday Inn, where the old lady froze in the street, and she had a younger woman with her. You said you tried to render assistance. In answer to my learned friend, you stated you did not photograph that incident, but did you make any kind of pictorial or other description of that? Did you record it in some way, that location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do have photographs of that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, after that incident, make any other kind of recordings of it? Did you in any way write about it, sketch it, or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When I went up to the Serb side one time, I found from quite a different position, even closer, the day I was there, the day they fired into the street, that was the street they were firing into from that Serb position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just wondering if, on the day of the incident, you made any particular record in your view, say you refer to your journal. Did you make any particular record of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I made --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you record as such that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I had gone out the front -- now, this is from recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry if I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to get as close as I can to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. I'm going to ask you not to try and retell the story, but did you write about it or did you do a sketch or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I wrote about it. I wrote about the girl and the woman and that the woman was fired upon and I went out in the street to bring her back in and I continue on about the Canadians coming. It's all in the journal, it's all there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. There's just one last thing that I would like to ask you, Mr. Ashton. This is in reference to the photograph you stated you took in September and was referred to in evidence in connection with the issue of the "iron cross." That was in fact, in your own exhibit, photo number 1328. In fact, Mr. Ashton -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On reflection, I'm not so sure that the question we were pondering will add anything significant, and in the interests of saving time as well, I think we can say that that concludes the re-examination. I'm obliged, Your Honours. The only thing I would now mention is the issue of tendering the relevant exhibits from the evidence of Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blaxill. As far as I'm aware of, we have at this moment documents that I would guess the parties would tender into evidence. First of all, the black-and-white map 3644. That's the big one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would suggest that that be entered into evidence as 3644.JA, to follow the previous method we used with that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if there's no objection against that, it's admitted into evidence. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think we have the bundle of photos, P3641.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bundle of photos. No objection. It's admitted in evidence. Then we have a marked map with number P3645 and 45.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: For the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the translation. That's the marked map, the smaller one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. So it's admitted into evidence. Then as far as the Defence is concerned, because I think these were all the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed. That's all I invite you to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then as far as the Defence is concerned, we have a statement of Roy Thomas, which I understand is tendered into evidence as Defence Exhibit D12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to that exhibit, I object to that tender for this reason: That the only part of it which was relevant to these proceedings was one, I think perhaps two sentences, which in any event were read onto the record. If, Mr. President, you think that nevertheless there should be a hard copy of those sentences, then that is what should be tendered into evidence, that is, those sentences. At the very most, the page, but certainly not the whole statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole statement. Would you please respond, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence is ready, if necessary, to photocopy, re-photocopy and re-re-photocopy all the pages of the dossier, of the file, but is it necessary? We have the relevant pages. The witness recognised his signature on the photographs. We have the dates because Mr. Ierace made a passionate response on the chronology of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I just ask you -- no, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The question is whether the Defence insists on tendering into evidence the statement of Roy Thomas or not or can just limit itself to one page. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... or you will insist?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is yes, Mr. President, to the question you have just asked. Our answer is yes, we will be tendering the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please respond to the objection. The objection was that only a few lines, or at most one page, was relevant, and the other parts should not be submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am of the opinion that everything should be tendered with respect to the context so that the Trial Chamber has the whole context to take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will decide on this issue after the break. We heard the objection. We'll take a decision on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have the photos to be tendered into evidence, I would say the photos of tanks, D13 up until D21, 21 included. Any objections? So that's admitted into evidence. And then we have photo D22, which is the photo of, I would say, the smoking car, if you would allow me this characterisation. That's D22. No objection. It's admitted. And then we have the last two photographs, of which I asked the Defence on whether they would like to have any markings on it. They said they would, but I did not notice any markings --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D23, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but these are the same photographs, as I see, as those that are in the bundle, so they are admitted into evidence as photos already, and since no markings are made, I would like to hear from the Defence what the reason is that they want a black and white photocopy of those photos already being admitted as exhibits will be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's all right. Thank you. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have to change again to the English. Let me just read your answer. So I do understand that they are not tendered into evidence and we rely on the statement of the witness as he has given on the coloured photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just, with your permission, make one more proposal for tendering into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to propose that the black-and-white map with the positions marked be tendered into evidence as a Defence exhibit. It would be D24. And the Defence would also like -- so that is the map with the positions marked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in response to questions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think both the markings of the witness, upon questions of the Prosecution and questions of the Defence, are marked on the same map, and they have been admitted as Exhibit 3644.JA. So I don't think that there's any need of admitting the same map with the same markings on it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I merely wished you to confirm that. The Defence has one more proposal. With your permission, the Defence would propose that all three statements given by Mr. Ashton to the investigators of the Prosecution be tendered under one number as a Defence exhibit, including both annexes, which were supplied with the statement to the Defence. The Defence apologises if photocopies are necessary, and the Defence will, in the course of the day, hand in a sufficient number of photocopied copies of this statement to the Registry. And I should ask that they be numbered with a single number. I think that that number would be D24, that that's the next number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from any objections, I first would like to note that it would not be D24, but it would be D23, the first number after D22, because the other photos have not been tendered into evidence. But do I understand there are objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed so, Your Honour. Essentially, my learned friend does not indicate precisely the reasons why she would wish to have the entirety of these statements, which means any additional photographs that have not been exhibited and so forth, placed before the Court. The evidence has been covered, and really and truly, the only certain specific extracts have been put to Mr. Ashton in cross-examination. Rather like my learned friend's observations regarding the other statement, I don't think it justifies a wholesale submission in evidence of all the statements of a witness if vast tracts of that have not in any way been put to the witness in the course of cross-examination, and I therefore ask, as a matter of relevance, that they should stick to the admission of -- or rather, submit to Your Honours to admit only those portions that are relevant to the cross-examination that have been raised in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence sees the relevance of these exhibits and would like to tender them as Defence exhibits in order to test the credibility of the witness, who has testified before this Tribunal over the past few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the tendering into evidence, in view of the objections, after the break. We will have, then, perhaps, the break a bit earlier than usual, and I would like to propose to you that we start again at 10.50, and we'll adjourn until then, after the witness has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10.55. Mr. Ashton, I'd like to thank you for coming here as a witness and informing the Court about things that happened in Sarajevo upon questioning of the examination of the parties. I still have to ask whether my colleagues have any additional questions to put to the witness. There are no additional questions, so, Mr. Usher, would you please guide Mr. Ashton out of the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we're almost at 10.30, so let's have a break until 11.00. We'll be adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber still had to decide on the tendering into evidence of both the statement of Roy Thomas and the statements given to the Prosecutors' investigators by Mr. Ashton. Our decision is that these statements may be tendered into evidence, but only to the extent that they are relating to the incidents or the specific subject touched upon during cross-examination. So not the whole statements, not just one page, because the subject might go from one page to the other, so that we can have a look at the context of this statement as far as the incident or the subject is concerned, but anything else, you don't have to delete it, but is not admitted into evidence and we'll pay only attention to those parts of this evidence which touches upon the issues dealt with during cross-examination. So it's not just the lines, a bit more, a bit of context, but not the whole statement. I think there are no other decisions to be taken at this moment. This would mean that the Prosecution may call the next witness. And as far as I understand from your list, it would be Alija Mulaomerovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, and that witness will be taken by Chester Stamp, who is two on my right. Present also at the bar table for the Prosecution at this moment is Manoj Sachdeva. He will assist us at the bar table. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one other issue. There are no exhibits, no documents which will be shown to the witness. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There is a map, that is the standard Sarajevo map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Standard Sarajevo map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which will be shown to the witness. Mr. President, whilst I'm on my feet, I go back briefly to the decision that you have just handed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The earlier statements refer to photographs which are not before the Chamber. There is an annexure to one of the statements which refers to each of a number of photographs. They were not included in the witness's final evidence because they either predate or post-date the indictment period. But since the decision is to allow the statements into evidence, Your Honours may wish to have the annexures and the photographs to which the annexures refer. If, following some deliberation, you could let us know that, then we will provide copies of those photographs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd first like to wait and see what parts of the statements the Defence will come up as being -- as touching upon the issues dealt with during cross-examination, and if it would be necessary for the understanding of the context to see the photographs. At this moment, I do not see yet any necessity, but just convince this Chamber and we'll give a decision on that. But for the time being, I would not insist on having any photographs with it, but we'll first see what the Prosecution will offer to this Chamber to be tendered into evidence, and then we'll have a look at whether this is really limited by context, and then we'll give a decision and we'll also see that any photographs are needed or not. May I also ask the parties whether -- and I'm now just looking a bit further than just the witness to be called -- that on the witness Hajir -- I have difficulties pronouncing it. Hajir, Sehbajraktarevic, Jusufovic, Witness B, Aernout Van Lynden and Morten Hvall - I just go to number 10 - are there any problems at this moment as far as disclosure of documents, translations, whatsoever there is? I would like to be informed about that. But I just wanted to remind you that I expect the parties to communicate well in advance to inform the Court if there are any problems. If this Court is not informed there are problems, we would not like to be confronted with it at the very moment of the witness being in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to Witness D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- a letter was forwarded by the Prosecution to the Defence yesterday, informing the Defence that there is an additional exhibit to be tendered through that witness, namely, a segment of the video which was shown during my opening. That's the only change, I think, to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There will be no problem as far as disclosure of this video is concerned. So then, Mr. Ierace, the Prosecution may call its next witness. Mr. Usher -- yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Your Honours. The next witness the Prosecution intends to call is Alija Mulaomerovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mulaomerovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome to this courtroom. You are called as a witness by the Prosecution. But before testifying, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you by the usher, and would you then please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mulaomerovic. Mr. Stamp will examine you, so please be seated. Mr. Stamp, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Alija Mulaomerovic. I'm from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are your professional qualifications, please?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm a physician by profession. I specialised in hygiene and organisation of health care. I am the director of Institute for Emergency, Medical Emergency Service in Sarajevo. I had that function during the war and I still occupy the same function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long have you been director of the emergency medical services in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I've been the director of the emergency medical services since 1987, without interruption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you were director during the war. This is the war of 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Throughout the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, immediately before the war, can you tell us what were the services provided by the Emergency Medical Centre, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The emergency medical service was organised for the benefit of the population of Sarajevo, including all the six of its municipalities which it had at the time and which were covered by our centre in relation to the overall number of ten municipalities that were considered to be the part of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of medical services did it provide to the population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The emergency medical service is in charge of providing medical protection and care to the individuals whose life or health are threatened or in cases where severe damage to health is likely to occur. That is, it provides medical help to all persons who are injured or wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where was the Emergency Medical Centre located?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The Emergency Medical Centre was located at the same location where it is today, that is, in Darovalaca krvi Street, number 14. The name of the street actually today is Kolodvorska, but the number is the same, number 14. That is the main building of the emergency medical service. We had four satellite stations belonging to our service, which were located in the municipalities of Vogosca, Ilidza, Novi Grad, Dobrinja, and the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the delivery of the medical services, did the Emergency Medical Centre have or use any particular equipment or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: In the course of its work, the Emergency Medical Centre uses ambulances which are equipped with the relevant equipment to provide emergency care during the transport itself and also on the premises belonging to the Emergency Medical Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as director, what were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: As the director, I am in charge for the overall organisation and the functioning of various departments of the service, including all matters relating to the staff and the premises themselves and the function that the medical centre is supposed to provide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the outbreak of hostilities in 1992, did you make any change in respect of the organisation of the centre?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. At the beginning of the war, we withdrew our staff from the outstations because they were under a blockade, and we centralised the work of the emergency service to the main building. That is, our staff was centralised and started working in the central building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by a "blockade"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: What I mean by a "blockade" is the fact that it was impossible to reach those outstations because they were under the control of Serb forces. I am referring to the outstations in Ilidza, Dobrinja, and Vogosca. It was physically impossible to reach those outstations, including the airport station, which was also cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the outbreak of the conflict in 1992, did your staff situation remain the same?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, most of the staff remained. However, there was a number of employees of Serb ethnicity that left the service. That is, they stopped coming from work as of the 4th of April. And in the course of the month of April, and later on in May, the number of staff was significantly -- that number of staff was significantly reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict, what was the ethnic composition of your staff?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The composition of my staff was multi-ethnic at all times. At the beginning of the conflict, our employees were members of all ethnic communities. I wouldn't be able to tell you the percentage but I'm sure that it duly reflected the ethnic composition of the population of the town of Sarajevo. I'm sure about that. All three ethnic communities were represented; Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, as they were referred to in those days. However, in the course of the conflict, the number of employees of Serb ethnicity was significantly reduced because, in most of the cases, they left the emergency medical service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect to the organisation of the functions of the Emergency Medical Centre, did you take any particular steps in respect to the ethnic composition of the staff?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: We did. At the beginning, our emergency teams, with ambulances, were usually stopped at the barricades and checkpoints, and that is the reason why, in organisational terms, we endeavoured to have multi-ethnic teams, to the extent it was possible. So the team would consist of a physician, a paramedic, and the driver, and we tried to see to it that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they were members of different ethnicities. So it was one way of having some sort of safeguards, that they would provide some kind of security to one another because of the barricades that were erected at the outbreak of the war by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe the Emergency Medical Centre premises at Kolodvorska Street.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: It is the central facility of the centre. It had several clinics for general medical intervention, emergency type of medical intervention. Then we had a clinic for surgical intervention and trauma, pediatric clinics, also for emergency cases, and we also have a diagnostic service, which included a laboratory, x-rays, and also a technical department and workshop, which also included a garage. There was also the administrative and legal department there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the building or buildings at Kolodvorska Street.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The building itself is quite large. Its surface area is about 3.000 square metres. Most of it is situated on the ground floor. That is, all medical facilities are on the ground floor, the reason for that being the emergency nature of the work, so that the vehicles could access all relevant departments. In the basement we had a garage, together with car workshops, vehicle maintenance workshops, and a car wash service as well, and some sanitary facilities that were located both on the ground floor and in the basement. As for the upper floors, we had the administrative, legal, and finance departments situated on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this building have any particular markings on it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The building was visibly marked. The name of the service was written in visible letters on the roof of the building. The "Institute for Emergency Medical Services" was written on the building, and it was duly marked with the international sign of the Red Cross, of the same dimensions. It was quite visible, and the cross itself was one metre large. Each of the entrances was also marked with the name of the relevant department written on it so it was visible from the outside. One could tell what each department stood for. The ground floor has a glassed-in area, so it was not protected very well except for the portions that were built in concrete walls. The roof was covered in cupolas, in domes, so that the natural light, daily light, could come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The markings of the International Red Cross and the name of the Emergency Medical Centre which were on the building, on the roof of the building, you said were visible. From about how far could these markings be seen?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I think that they could be seen from a distance of up to one kilometre, I think, especially during the night, because they were in neon. The markings were in neon light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you operated ambulances. Could you describe these ambulances, please. Did they have any particular markings?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Our vehicles were Citroen C-25 type vehicles, which is a large ambulance, and then the Volkswagen C-15 vehicles were used, and then I think we had two Mercedes as well. But all of these vehicles were visibly marked with the name of the firm. It said SOUR UNHCR, the University Medical Centre. We were part of that, and the work organisations included the clinics. And under that, it said OUR, Organisation of Associated labour, and the Institute for Medical Emergency -- for the Medical Emergency Service Sarajevo. That's what it said on the vehicles. And then it said "Ambulance," with the Red Cross emblem on the sides of the vehicle and at the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the war started in early 1992, was the building affected?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The building was hit several times during the war. I can't tell you when it was hit first, but it is common knowledge that the building was hit several times directly. It received direct hits at the entrance to the building and the courtyard and part of the street outside the building, and the roof of the building as well, because it's a flat roof, a concrete flat roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "hit," what do you mean? You said the building was hit several times. Hit by what?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: It was hit with artillery projectiles from artillery weapons and infantry weapons, artillery shells and infantry weapons, as far as I'm able to explain this technically. We referred to them as infantry projectiles and grenades or artillery shells. That's how we referred to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "infantry weapons"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean small arms; snipers, rifles, that kind of thing, weapons which are able to shoot individually, individual bullets, and a burst of gunfire as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did this shelling and sniping affect your staff when the conflict began?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Of course it did. It was a direct threat to their security and the safety of the staff, because they were directly exposed to danger. Their lives were directly threatened and they had to do their job. They had to give first aid and emergency service to the injured and wounded citizens, whereas they were placing their life at risk as well. So their lives were at risk and the lives of their patients were at risk while the shelling was going on and while there was gunfire from the small arms and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suffer any casualties among your staff in the early period of the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, we did have casualties. Some were wounded and some were also killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to turn your attention to the period beginning August of -- I beg your pardon. September of 1992 to August of 1994. In that period, did the shelling of the hospital stop or did it continue?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: From September 1992 onwards, this just meant a continuation of what had been going on. Things continued with the same intensity in the Kolodvarska Street.
