It was the same for the personnel and for the ambulances. They came under fire. And on the 17th of September, in fact, part of a shell hit a driver, some shrapnel hit a driver. His name was Zika Lazic, the driver's name, and it was in the street outside the emergency service, and it was the regional service that was located within our own building. On the 19th of September, a sniper hit another staff member, whose name was Nurko Milic, and he was hit when he was taking a patient inside on a stretcher. He was transporting the patient from the ambulance into the building, into the emergency service building. He was hit at the entrance to the building. And he remained a serious invalid. One of his kidneys had to be amputated. He is retired now as a serious invalid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first incident you spoke of, of the 17th of September, when a shell hit the driver, what was the driver doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I think he was a pedestrian at the time. He was walking towards the building to go to his office, and I think he was hit by a shell from a close distance. And we had to perform an amputation on one of his legs. He was taken care of in the emergency service, and thanks to the fact that he was close by at the time, we were able to save his life. Otherwise, he would probably have died. Today he is also a serious invalid with just one leg. The other was amputated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any military facilities inside the Emergency Medical Centre compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't any military facilities. The institute is a civilian health facility. It was like that before the war, during the war, and today as well. It is a civilian facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it well known in Sarajevo that it was a civilian medical facility prior to the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I think that everybody in Sarajevo and even children knew that it was a civilian medical facility, because the citizens would set a portion of their personal incomes to finance the building. So in fact it was through citizens' contributions that the medical emergency centre was built in the first place, to cater to emergency cases. It was built in 1980 and put into operation that same year. So it's a relatively new facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you say where the sniping at the hospital and its environs came from?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: We think it came from the area where the former police school at Vrace was located. That's one part. And the other section was the Ozrenska Vrbovska street area, Zagorska street or Hrasno Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These two areas that you speak of, under which party's control were they?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Under the control of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the shelling of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has an objection. The question asked of the witness was about the two parts of town, two sections of town. I think that my colleague ought to be more specific and precise in asking his question, what he's actually referring to, if I understood him correctly. The witness didn't speak about sections of town; he spoke about the police school and Ozrenska Street and Hrasno Brdo. Perhaps my learned colleague could rephrase his question and ask what part of town those facilities are. More precision, please, that's my basic objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first see what has been said. The question put by Mr. Stamp was: "Now can you say where the sniping at the hospital and its environs came from?" The answer was: "We think it came from the area where the former police school at Vrace was located. That's one part. And the other one was the..." then it doesn't mention the name of the street "... area of Zagorska street or Hrasno Brdo. " The next question was: "These two areas--"

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "These two areas that you speak of, under which party's control were they?" I think the witness has spoken about areas, one area, Vrace area, and the other one the Hrasno Brdo. I do understand that that's an area as well, but if I'm mistaken, please, Mr. Mulaomerovic, correct me.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Vrace area is a well-known district, quarter of the town. That's where it is and that's where the police academy or school was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Hrasno Brdo also an area of town?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Hrasno Brdo too is a quarter of the town, but the most precise location would be to say that it was Ozrenska and Vrbovska and Zagorska street. Perhaps it doesn't belong to Hrasno Brdo actually, but those are the streets. I know the streets, Ozrenska, Vrbovska, and Zagorska. Those were the actual streets. Whether it actually belongs to Hrasno Brdo I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Keeping this in mind, Mr. Stamp, would you please proceed and, if necessary, rephrase your question. But I think the objection as such is denied, but let's try to avoid any disputes on minor issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect to the shelling of the hospital of the Emergency Medical Centre and its environs, can you say where the shelling originated from?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a location for the shelling. The shelling came from all directions, I think, so it's difficult to say. All we know is that there was shelling from somewhere, and we also know that we were subject to direct fire and that our lives were in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period September 1992 to August 1994, was a building damaged as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I said we had a flat roof. The emergency service had a flat roof, and it was insulated with hydro insulation, and the results of the shells that exploded on it was that the roof was damaged so that when it rained, the water would flow directly inside the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period, did you undertake any repairs of the building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: We improvised, as far as we could, the hydro insulation, but all the glass surfaces around the building were destroyed. But we did do repairs and we did them in the course of the night. We came by some bituminka tar and closed the holes, the apertures that had been formed on the roof, to prevent the water from coming in and to protect the building so that we could continue our work, as far as we were able, and to keep the rooms dry. We closed off the glass partitions using wooden planks or boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court why you did these repairs at night.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: That was the only time we could do the repairs, when it was dark, when we were under cover of darkness, when the night protected us; otherwise, we would be a sitting target to firing from artillery weapons and small arms. We would have been quite visible up there. So that was the only way we could repair the building. It was impossible to do that during the day, so we had to use the night and do it under cover of darkness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall if there were any particular types of shells which struck the building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we used to refer to them as shells from mortars, mortar shells. That's what we used to call them. And then the big ones, I really don't know what they were called, those big ones. If I say that they were shells, artillery shells, with a diameter of 40 -- about 40 millimetres and then there would be larger ones too, and there was a special one that -- I think that would have been a sort of tracer which hit the building on the 4th of December, 1992. The tracer bullets -- so tracer bullets were used, and then these guided shells as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "guided shells"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by the remains of those shells, what it looked like was a long spiral. There was a long spiral, wire spiral, and the action of it is continuous. That's how they explained it to us laymen. They would be able to target a certain -- to aim at a certain target. So in some places, we saw the remains of this coil or spiral wire. And that particular shell hit the gynaecological department, gynaecological ward, and destroyed the whole area. Luckily, at that particular time, nobody was in the room so there were no human casualties. It was just a great psychological shock to everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period September 1992 to August 1994, under what conditions did the ambulances operate?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: From September 1992, and in 1993, the first half of 1993, that was the most difficult period, the worst period for us. We found it very difficult to work under the conditions that prevailed during that period. We worked under impossible conditions. We lacked everything. We had insufficient electricity supply, we didn't have enough water, we worked without water, without gas. It was cold. Temperatures were low. There was no heating. We had no fuel. Different types of fuel were lacking. And we even had patients who displayed symptoms of frostbite as a result of the extremely low temperatures, the extreme cold, the harsh conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a moment, let us speak about the ambulances. During this period, were the ambulances affected by the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were. Our ambulances were not able to transport patients during the day, when there was intensive shelling. We had to treat our patients in out-patient departments. We had to stabilise their condition, to give them first aid, and to keep them alive until such a time as they were able to be transported in an ambulance, that is to say, during the night, and we were to follow set routes. We referred to them as the war route, war ambulance route. We had to use by-streets and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. back streets to reach the hospital at Kosevo, where the patients were treated further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just clarify that? The emergency medical service, you said, provides emergency medical treatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you keep patients at the medical centre for any prolonged period of time after their condition has stabilised?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: We are not a hospital institution, so we treat patients prior to their being hospitalised. So our interventions imply the administration of emergency primary medical treatment, on the spot where the accident or injury has taken place or where a person has been taken ill. So our interventions took place in localities where people were wounded and injured, and our teams would go out to those localities and evacuate the casualties to the central emergency service facility, where the patients would be given emergency first aid, reanimation, resuscitation. We would check bleeding, any bleeding, stop bleeding, and then undertake the necessary measures while the patient was being transported, medical intervention during transport. Let me just add: We would replace the bodily fluids that a patient had lost. Drips, we would administer intravenous drips to stabilise the patient and ensure that his primary bodily functions were working. And under this intensive treatment, serious patients were then transported to hospitals, where they were hospitalised and treated further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could you tell us how the transport of these patients to the hospital was organised?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: As I've said, transport always took place during the night, without any lights on the vehicles. The lights were switched off. And we would have to use the back way, the byroads and back streets, which meant that we -- it usually took a longer period of time. We weren't able to use the main roads; they were dangerous and open to artillery fire. So we had to take the back streets. And they were taken to the main entrance at Kosevo Hospital and later on to the State Hospital, which was the former medical military hospital. We had to go via Hum hill, which is a bypass, because we weren't able to drive past the Marsala Tito barracks, which was on the main road. So we couldn't use any of the main roads, we had to take the back streets. Vojvode Putnika was another main road which we couldn't use at that time. So we had to take an indirect route, using safer streets. That's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if you would allow me. You might have heard that we are trying to gain a bit of discipline in this court, and just in order to assist you, I'd like to inform you that, up until now, you used half of the time which was the estimate for this witness. I'm not -- so this is just to assist you, nothing else. I'm just drawing your attention to that fact. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned two staff members who were injured by sniping and one by shelling. During the period I referred to, were there any others that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: As I said, on the 17th of September Zika was wounded. On the 19th of September, Nurko Milic was wounded; and on the 23rd of September, two of our employees were wounded, Dragoje, Mario Dragoje and Marko Dragoje, a father and a son who had a workshop and we had a contract with them. They were in charge of maintaining our vehicles. And they moved their workshop from the Darovalaca krvi street and eventually took up quarters in the basement of our building. The two of them were wounded by shrapnel in their apartment, at number 9 of Darovalaca krvi Street, on the 19th floor. Both of them were severely injured and received injuries to the stomach. And I believe that he, the son, was evacuated to England for treatment. I think he's still there, actually. That took place on the 18th -- 23rd of September. And then on the 18th of October -- I was just going to tell you about the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on. Tell us about the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year is this? 18th of October of which year?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: 18th of October, 1992. I'm talking about 1992 now. So on the 18th of October, our medical technician was wounded, Salko Kahrimanovic. He was wounded by shrapnel of a shell in front of the emergency medical service building. Salko Kahrimanovic. And on the 19th of October, an ambulance driver was wounded. His name was Rafet Cikotic. He was wounded in Partizanska Street. So not in the immediate vicinity of the medical centre, Emergency Medical Centre, but in Partizanska Street. But he was wounded as an ambulance driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the medical centre itself have any facilities for keeping bodies, dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a morgue which was situated in the basement, just one room. However, very often there was not enough space for all the casualties. Also because the evacuation of the casualties, that is, the fatalities, was not properly organised, so very often we were buried with bodies, not only the area surrounding the morgue, but also the adjacent corridors and the space around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- please tell us: In the period that I'm speaking about, September 1992 to August 1994, what was the flow of casualties into the Emergency Medical Centre?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The flow of casualties was somewhat less serious than at the very beginning, mid-1992, because local clinics have managed to organise themselves in the meantime, and they operated locally, in various neighbourhoods, which to a certain extent facilitated our work. The only patients we had were the people who were wounded in the immediate vicinity of the centre. Actually, when I say "the immediate vicinity," I'm referring to the area of about several kilometres away from the building, from the main location of the Emergency Medical Centre. The maximum number of daily patients was up to 50. I'm referring to the severely wounded casualties. Whereas at the very beginning, we had over a hundred patients admitted per day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say at about what proportion of these patients were military and what proportion were civilian?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I couldn't, because in view of the nature of the work and the philosophy behind our work, we admitted not only injured people, but also people who had sustained some general type of trauma and had other types of health problems. So whoever needed our help was treated humanely. And not only casualties, but everybody in medical need. But I remember that there were quite a few of them who were members of the armed forces, because of the kinds of documents that they had with them. But they would have been wounded while off duty, while they were simply walking down the street, and got injured. So they were also our patients. Everybody who had experienced some kind of -- this kind of misfortune, that is, whoever needed our help, was treated in our medical centre. As for the records, others were in charge of that, and they knew about the official status of patients who were admitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you say if there were any psychological effects which the sniping and the shelling had on your staff?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were such moments when the entire staff would experience this kind of psychological trauma and had difficulties to cope with the kind of situation that we were faced with and the kind of hell we were living in at that time, especially in cases of loss of colleagues. For example, on the 31st of February [as interpreted], a colleague of ours was hit by a sniper bullet, Ramiz Komilija. I forgot to tell you about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: 31st of February [as interpreted], 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: So he was hit from a sniper, and the bullet hit his spine. He succumbed to the consequences of this wounding six months later, and he was completely paralysed during those six months. He lived only thanks to artificial lungs. But eventually, he died. There were cases where people would start crying, all of them at the same time, and such moments were unbearable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And speaking as a doctor and as a human being, did you make any observations as to the psychological effect that the shelling and sniping had on the people that you came across with day to day?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Some of the employees underwent severe stress, and many of them were not able to continue with their work. I remember Avdo Beglerovic, a driver of ours, who at one point in time said that he was no longer able to continue working there, that he didn't feel physically capable to continue. So he was spared. And I told my employees, I told them that whoever is not feeling up to it should not come to work, so as not to influence adversely other staff members. We were relying on the strongest ones, those who were able to endure it all, both physically and psychologically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did they react to this stress and trauma that you described?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: In most of the cases, people would start crying, moaning, making various types of comments, or simply they would become depressed. They were desperate, the situation was desperate, and they verbally expressed it. They spoke about the situation as the one without any possible solution. And as I said, we appealed to those who were the strongest ones to continue coming to work, and we told others not to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the population of Sarajevo in general, did you observe any effects of the stress on that population?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to observe such effects on the population. I remember that there were cases of mass withdrawal of population from the front lines. Most of the people gathered in the centre of the town. So there were periods of time where population would move from one neighbourhood of the town to another in large numbers. We were aware of the state of panic which reigned amongst the people, but we were also aware of the fact that we simply must endure, not to demoralise the population as a whole, because, for them, we constituted some kind of support, not only technically speaking, but also morally, and we wanted to encourage people with our work and continue. We simply could not stop because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of your work, Doctor, have you yourself and the Emergency Medical Centre received any particular award for its work?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: In 1996, immediately after the war, the cantonal assembly, or rather, the parliament of the Sarajevo canton, awarded our institute with the so-called 6th of April award, which is the most prestigious award that the society has been traditionally giving ever since the Second World War, but that's the first time that this award was given to a medical institution, to the Emergency Medical Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the award for?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: It is a recognition, both professionally and politically. It can be awarded to an individual or to an organisation. In this case, it was awarded to an organisation, to the Emergency Medical Centre of Sarajevo, as a recognition for our work during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you or the centre received any international recognition for the work that you did during the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I personally received an award by the Pan-European Centre for Emergency Medical Management Systems Foundation. It is an international organisation which awarded me, in 1998, as a physician, as a humanist, and as a professional who carried on with his work during the war and also immediately after the war. I was awarded this special recognition in Opatija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And lastly: During the period of the war, were any weapons allowed in the hospital, the Emergency Medical Centre compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that we had such cases. I issued a very strict order to the effect that no weapons whatsoever should be brought inside the building, and the medical staff should not possess any weapon, the penalty being suspension from work should anyone try to bring in weapons and use them during the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we come close to the time when we'll have a break. If you please could find a suitable moment to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is a convenient time now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is now a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I also, just again in assisting you, remind you that we are now at 75 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I have been told that by my colleagues here at the bar. I'm grateful nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 20 minutes, so we resume at 20 minutes to 1.00. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do you propose that we continue, then, with Witness B, number 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then later you'll inform us about what time you intend to call the witness which is not available at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Stamp, you would like to continue cross-examining the -- examining the witness. I'll ask the usher to bring him in. Thank you. Mr. Mulaomerovic -- yes. Please be seated, Mr. Mulaomerovic. You may proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the examination-in-chief of the witness is concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Of course. I thought I corrected myself already. Yes, please. It's concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't understand you. I thought it was continued. So then the Defence will have the opportunity to start the cross-examination of Mr. Mulaomerovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mulaomerovic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd, 24th of June, 1999, you made a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal; is that correct, and you signed your statement, right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Correct, as it states there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The things you set out in the statement are those things that you declared to the investigators of the Tribunal, and it was then written down, and you confirmed that that was so?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today that the centre or Institute for Emergency Medical Assistance is located in Darovalaca krvi Street.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The street's name today is in Kolodvarska Street, and it used to be Darovalaca krvi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kolodvarska is its name now?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that you said that it was in Darovalaca krvi Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to us where Kolodvarska Street is located in the city of Sarajevo. Could you give us a closer indication of whether it is the centre of town, whether it is a suburb? Could you be more specific in locating the street?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The building is in the centre, if you look at the overall city of Sarajevo, the urban area. It is located close to important public municipal buildings. The electrical distribution network building and the 20-storey high-rise, which is the pension fund and social insurance building. And also close by is another tall building, the Energoinvest high-rise, and another one that is is popularly called the matchstick, another high-rise building, in fact. Then there is the stadium. It's a railway stadium, and that is 500 metres away. It is the Zeljeznicar football club stadium on the opposite side of the Miljacka River, whereas our facility is on the right side of the Miljacka River, on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mulaomerovic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, all the buildings that you mentioned in respect to your facility, were they high-rise buildings? Were they higher than your building or lower ones?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No. They were all higher than our own building. They are all high-rise buildings, higher than ours, 20 storeys, except for the electrical distribution network building, which is only a four-storey building. But all the others were 20 storeys high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your institute - and we're referring to the period before the war, that's how my learned colleague started off -- can you be more specific and tell us when you think the war in Sarajevo began? When would you say it began?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the emergency service it began between the 4th and 56th April, 1992. That's when we considered that the war for us started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that before the war, as an institute, you had four outstations.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you: They are the Vogosca, Novi Grad, and Ilidza and Dobrinja outstations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Novi Grad is Dobrinja. It's the Novi Grad municipality, but the locality is Dobrinja. And the fourth was at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The airport, I see. Before the war broke out, you say before the 4th and 5th of April, what happened to those four stations?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Those four outstations worked -- they were on duty during the night and catered to the needs of the population in the course of the night, emergency service and general medical services, when the health clinics or centres were closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the medical staff, in your own centre - and when I say "your centre," I mean the building in Kolodvarska Street - and in the outstations, before the war, before the 4th and 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: It was mostly a tri-national composition, made up of the three ethnic groups: Muslims, Serbs and Croats, or whichever order you like to take those in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both at the outstations and the central building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because it was the rule that the outstations weren't actually detached, but for a period of one month, we were to have one team located there, and then this would be recycled. And teams would replace each other every month in the outstations. They would be replaced on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This national or ethnic composition, was it retained after the outbreak of the war? Because we've just been speaking about before the war.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It did. It remained the same. Nobody was sacked, nobody was left without a job unless an individual had decided to give up his job and leave the emergency service institution. We even took in new members, new staff members, during the war, Serbs amongst them too, although the majority left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the majority left," do you mean in the outstations too and the main building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because all the staff members came to the central building when the other outstations were cut off and placed under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What outstations remained under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The Vogosca, Ilidza, and airport outstation, whereas Dobrinja, the Dobrinja station, was shelled and destroyed, and it was within the frameworks of what was called Vojnicko Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when the Dobrinja station was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Straight away, at the beginning. I don't remember the exact date, but it's probably recorded somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to follow, there was fighting. How was the outstation destroyed? How did that happen? How did it come about?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was destroyed largely from the shelling, and it remains like that today. Only a third of the building has been reconstructed and repaired; otherwise the rest still remains in ruins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I said that it was at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Vogosca and Ilidza outstations? What happened to them? You said that they were under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ethnic composition of the staff members in those outstations remain the same?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the composition was always mixed, ethnically speaking, and as I say, the workers formed teams and each team would spend a certain amount of time working in the outstations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that what happened after the conflict broke out as well?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was just a sort of mathematical, arithmetical record and list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today, in response to a question by my learned friend, on line 6, 7, and 8, that you withdrew the staff from the stations in the periphery, in the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: That's right. We said that all our staff members should come to the central building so that we could group our forces, our staff, and see who we had available and then send out people to intervene when the call-up came for a medical intervention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took that decision?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I did myself, as director, because otherwise it was impossible to organise our work and to work in the outstations that were under Serb control. It was not possible to access them. They were completely cut off. They were blocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who of the medical staff remained in those outstations, if they did? Do you happen to know? And what ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any information that people stayed in those outstations. Perhaps some of them did. Somebody did spontaneously if they failed to turn up at the main building. But the outstations were extinguished at the same time that the war broke out, to all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about the equipment that you had and the vehicles you had. Could you tell us how all that functioned, how it all operated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Our ambulances, vehicles, had all the medical and technical equipment required to act in emergency situations, and the vehicles remained in the central building; that is to say, they would go to these points daily, according to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the vehicles -- were the vehicles also sent to the Vogosca and Ilidza outstations?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, from the day central station, they would go off at night to do their shift, from 7.00 p.m. to 8.00 a.m. the following morning, during the night, and then they would return to the central building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether this was the system that was in operation before the war and during the war, or were there any changes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same principle remained the same during the war as it had been before the war. Daily, our vehicles, with the teams, would go to the outstations in Vogosca, Ilidza, Dobrinja, and the airport station, and we have new outstations today at the level of the canton of Sarajevo. That was the city of Sarajevo, now it is the canton, where we have the Ilijas, Trnovo, and Hadzici night stations, all the nine municipalities, in fact, which make up the administrative whole, which is the canton of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps I wasn't specific enough. When I said "before the war," I meant before the conflict broke out and the date you mentioned, before the 4th of April and after the 4th of April. Were those Vogosca and Ilidza stations functioning with respect to vehicles and equipment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 4th of April, all the outstations were in operation. They had all the necessary vehicles, they were manned with the necessary staff members and equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I've already answered that. They were all -- they all withdrew to the central building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the ethnic composition of your institution was mixed. Did that mean that all those who were Serbs in Ilidza and Vogosca came -- I'm thinking of the staff, the doctors and drivers and nurses, did they all come to the central building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the 4th of April, our records show that practically everybody came to the central institute, the central building. Not 100 per cent. Several people did not turn up, and I have their names down in our records. So not everybody did at the start of the aggression. They just stayed at home and didn't come to work, the people that didn't turn up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you kept records. Did you do that personally or some member of your institution?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: We have a brigade system or shift system. Each shift has a shift leader, and he records when people come to work, and they are responsible doctors in their shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serb physicians existed in the employ of your institute?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to give an exact figure. I'll be speaking off the bat, because I don't have the exact figures. But as far as I remember, I think there were 13, but don't hold me to that. We can check it out, if you want to know the exact number of Serb doctors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I was able to gather, you have books or records of your staff members, at the beginning of the conflict and during the conflict in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't keep the records on the basis of ethnic affiliation, but just the employees, how many employees and staff members we have, the numbers, according to the different categories: Doctors, nurses, technicians, drivers, and miscellaneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I was not thinking of the ethnic composition. All I wanted you to confirm was what I asked you, and you have confirmed that, the number of employees. Thank you. Would you explain to us how you admitted an individual to your institution.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: All calls for emergency medical intervention come in through one telephone number, 94 and 611, and the exchange operator, the dispatcher, answers those calls and sends teams, emergency teams, to the spot where medical assistance is required. So people call up two numbers, 94 and 611, and the calls are answered by a dispatcher. It's a special telephone that reaches the switchboard, the operator who dispatches the teams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an admissions log, log book?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The dispatcher would keep a protocol, or log book, for all calls and admissions. But later on, the telephone lines went down. They weren't operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep a protocol book of admissions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We did keep the protocol books in the dispatcher centre, in the admissions room, and we would record everybody coming in or brought in, in whichever way, whether by ambulance or private vehicles, who were brought in to the emergency centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you enter -- what were the entries you made into the protocol?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: We would write down the particulars and anamnesis, case history, why the person was being admitted, what their symptoms were. And then there was a dispatcher's book, log, where they would record the calls, the symptoms, and the location for which the emergency assistance is required, as well as the particulars of each individual; their name and surname, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you record the time of admittance?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the date?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a separate form that has to be filled in with the time, the date, and all the particulars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that protocol exist for 1992, 1993, and 1994? Is it still in existence? Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the protocol book exists, with all the particulars and entries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you admitted a patient, did you record whether he was a civilian or a soldier or a member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we made those entries. Perhaps this was done subsequently, but I don't think we would make those sorts of entries in that protocol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a patient was admitted to your institution who had been wounded by a firearm, were you duty-bound to report cases of that kind; and if so, who did you report cases of that kind to?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't report them. We would just write this down as a diagnosis. If it was vulnus sclopetarium, an entrance-exit wound, or perhaps if it was a wound, an injury caused by an explosive device, we would write it in as a diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your duty and obligation to make a report of people coming in with these types of injuries and report this to the competent authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I think we informed the police, that the police was informed of these war injuries, but I don't think that was done on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say not on a "regular basis," as far as you were able to notice, how often was this? Was it every month, every week, or every day? How often would this be done?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't reported on a regular basis, because that was impossible. If you had a hundred patients every day suffering from injuries or wounds, or even 50 patients, it would make this reporting impossible. So -- because it would take up too much time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were the director of the institution. Could any third persons have access to the protocol books without permission from you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, only official personnel, but not private individuals. So the police, the court authorities, they were able to gain access, but not anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to me how they were able to gain an insight into those protocols and who has to give permission?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: They make a request on the basis of -- they identify themselves and show cause. This can also be requested by a family member, for example. A family member might seek information about somebody who was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. killed. They could look in the records kept on the deaths, if they thought that it might be a family member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "the competent authority," could you explain whether the authorities can just have insight into the protocols or whether they could avail themselves of them and take them out?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody was able to take the books away, but they could just look at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that since 1987 you have been the institution's director. Now, from that time on, from 1987 to the present day, and especially in the period of 1992, 1993, and 1994 and 1995, whether you issued any documents to anybody with respect to those years, or whether anybody looked through the documents and books for those years?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I didn't give permission for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your indulgence and permission, I should like to present the witness with a Prosecution Exhibit that I received from my learned friends. I'm going to let the witness have a look at this document and to tell me whether this is the stamp of the Institute for Emergency Medical Assistance and whether he has any knowledge pertaining to the issuing of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Usher. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My learned friend, for the record, has described the document as an exhibit. I was wondering if we could be told what exhibit number it is in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's still a document, or is it a document that has been tendered into evidence? Because we have an agreement that we are only talking about exhibits once they've been admitted into evidence. Ms. Pilipovic, could you please give the number and tell us whether it's a document or an exhibit already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a document which was disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution as part of the documents listed on the 3rd of December, 2001 list. It's 00983141. That is the number of the document. And it is a list of names, actually, names of people who, according to this document, were admitted to the Institute for Emergency Medical Assistance on the 1st, on the 2nd, on the 5th, 7th, and 10th of October. I should like the witness to have a look at this document so that he can explain to us what kind of paper this is, in view of the fact that the document bears a stamp but no signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I assume that you tender this document into evidence? It would then be prenumbered D -- I'm just looking to the registrar. D24. Mr. Usher, could you please first bring the copies to the registrar. It has not yet been numbered, or is it numbered?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, this document will be marked as D24.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Could you please give one copy to the witness and other copies to the -- or is this just one copy you've got? The Bench would like to have -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a number of copies for the Chamber and also for the other party, and the registry, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have a document in front of you which bears the stamp belonging to the Institute for Emergency Medical Assistance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I said that persons in official capacity can have access to the documents, and this is a proof that the documents were accessed to by persons in official capacity. And when I say "persons in official capacity," I'm referring to the relevant authorities, such as the police, the judiciary, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards this particular document, do you know who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I know that individuals in official capacity gained insight into this documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether they made such inquiries for the period 1992 up to 1995? Throughout that period of time or only at certain points in time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I know that such inquiries were made by persons acting in official capacity throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, as the head of the institute, establish that such individuals were able to review these documents, and in what way were they able to gain access to such documents, documents which included the names of wounded persons and diagnoses, and so on and so forth, and over what period of time did they last?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: They were acting in official capacity, and as such, they were given our permission to gain access and insight into such documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they introduce themselves as persons acting in official capacity? Did you have any obligation to see their actual identification documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the record, as I have it, at page 72, line 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Stamp. I have some problems in finding page 72, since I'm still at 70, I think. Oh, the other -- yes, I'm -- I can't move the other one, so -- you said 72, line 23. Yes, it's -- yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The answer doesn't seem to follow on from the question, and I'm wondering if there is -- or if there might be a problem in the translation. If the question perhaps could be asked again so we could clarify what exactly is meant, if it please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question who compiled the document, since the answer is not very much -- it seems not to respond to the question. Now it's off my screen. I have to try to find it again. I think the question was: "As regards this particular document, do you know who compiled this document?" Is that the line you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On my computer transcript, it says: "No, I do not know." And that's in my recollection what the translation told us. And then the answer continues: "I know that individuals in official capacity gained insight." So I think a small part of the answer has fallen out on the main screen, but I see it on my computer that the answer is: "No, I don't know." Does that clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you will allow me. My feeling is that the second question which immediately followed was not recorded. I think that she asked who were those individuals in question. There seems to be -- or rather, it is possible that there has been an omission in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that. Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in trying to solve the problem. Is the Prosecution, having read the transcript as it is on the portable computer, has it solved the problem??

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the interests of time, we propose that the proceedings continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we need to clarify, we will do so later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can always check on the original recording. So please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know which individuals acting in official capacity made this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not. All I can tell you is that we are a public institution, and as such, we are open, and our work is such that it obliges us to provide access to the individuals acting in official capacity to our documentation. But in principle, I'm not interested in the identity of such individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we therefore agree that any individual who introduces him or herself as an individual acting in official capacity can gain entry into your institution and can be given access to your documentation with your permission?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if he or she produces the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is exactly what I would like to know. What kind of document must such individuals show to you upon coming to your institute?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: It is not something that we have to establish. Every public institution has its set of identifying documents, and from such documents we can see that the individual is acting indeed in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of this particular document, what kind of institution was this individual from?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not checking on them. They are working in accordance with their task, with their mission, and we have to be open, as an institution, to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know which individual it was who came to your institution and made this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is authorised, on behalf of your institution, to place a stamp on this type of document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The stamp is used in accordance with the relevant regulations governing the use of stamp. I don't know who exactly is authorised. Whoever has a signature of the director to that effect. If not, then it means that he is not authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who in your institution was authorised by yourself to use the official stamp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: The stamp was used by the legal department. I believe it is the secretary -- yes, the secretary of the director who uses the stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who in your institution is in charge of verifying, or rather, authenticating the information contained in the protocol, the information which was taken by this individual acting in official capacity for his own purposes? Who is authorised to confirm the authenticity of such information?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No one is specifically authorised to that effect, that is, to verify the authenticity of the documentation. The original documents are contained in the book of protocols, and this can be checked by anyone who wishes to have such access.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who on behalf of your institution is authorised to use this protocol that you're saying is an original document and to issue it to a third party or to an individual in official capacity, and who can testify to the veracity, to the authenticity of the copy of such documentation?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No one in particular. This is usually done by the relevant judicial body at the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, the one that is in front of you, bears only the stamp of your institution, and you are saying that you do not know who placed this stamp and that you don't know who was authorised to check the document against the original protocol. So in view of that, can you claim that these documents that are in front of you are consistent with the original, that is, with the protocol which is kept at your institution?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about the authenticity of such documents. That can be checked against the book of protocols, against the originals that are kept at the institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you yourself cannot confirm for us that the document that is in front of you, the document which bears the stamp of your institution, that these individuals listed under these numbers and described with these times of admission and relevant diagnoses - and we have a note that in each case the wound was sustained in an armed conflict - that this document is consistent with the original which is contained in the book of protocols?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. We are -- we do not have any superior position in respect of such authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had this document been certified or authenticated by the relevant authorities - as you say, a judicial body of some sort - would it be possible to claim that this document is then consistent with the original?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Such individual, I guess, is able to confirm that the document is indeed consistent with the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that your employees went out to locations upon receiving telephone calls to that effect. Line 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- since you seem to be touching upon a new subject, I'd like to inform you and assist you in a similar way as to the Prosecution, that you spent approximately 60 per cent of the time used in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you stated, at 12 hours, 02 minutes, that your teams would go out into locations in cases of wounding. What exactly did you mean when you said "wounding in war"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to the calls made to the dispatcher, who would inform us of the war activities and the casualties, and we would receive such information through them, or we would simply respond to these type of calls, in cases of shelling or wounding, involving either individual citizens or groups of citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would then visit the scene in an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The location would be specified - for example: "Pere Kosorica square, several individuals wounded. Please come as quickly as possible to provide medical help."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you then make a record of that particular location?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the duty of the dispatcher to record this kind of information. I mean, it wasn't myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the dispatcher go to the locations which were not specified? Were there such situations as well?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's very few locations which can be called as unspecified. Each dispatcher was able to specify and give appropriate indications about the location in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, you told us you had as many as a hundred patients admitted per day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 8th of June, I remember we had 107 patients altogether, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me quote from your statement that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal, page 6 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 3. "For example, at the time of severe combats for Pofalici, when Serbs tried to cut the city in two, a number of people were taken to the Institute for Emergency Medical Service."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, but we have not been given the references in the English statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. The wounded would sometimes be brought in piles to the emergency centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to the time when such combats were being conducted for Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It took place in the month of May, sometime in mid-May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what factions were opposed in this combat?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, those who were attacking the city against those who were defending the city. The attackers were attacking everything, all kinds of facilities in the town, including schools and other public institutions. Dr. Silva Rizvanbegovic was killed in a vehicle which was riddled with bullets coming from the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically in respect of Pofalici, could you be more specific and tell us where exactly that neighbourhood is in respect -- in relation to the centre of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: It is located near the tobacco factory, but we only had information that severe fighting was going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the ethnic composition of the population in the Pofalici neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not. I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I put to you that 80 per cent of the population was Serb, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you say so, I can, I think, believe you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, are you talking about 80 per cent of the population of Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asking about the Pofalici neighbourhood, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if the witness has answered the question to the extent that he has no knowledge, "I don't have any such information," I will not allow you to put a question again which results in the witness saying, "If you say so." The answer is given to your question. You can't just repeat it again, trying to either another answer or someone who has said he has no knowledge about it, to put the same question to him. So I will not allow you to do that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who was involved in the fierce fighting in the month of May in the Pofalici neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I told you that the fighting was between those who were attacking the city and those who were defending the city, involving us who were going about their daily work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, who defended the city? How did they identify themselves? Did they identify themselves as the defenders of the town and did have they have any common denominator, anything characteristic about them? In particular, did they wear any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: I can refer to them only as the citizens of Sarajevo who were defending their town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, who was the opposing party?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I'm sorry to interrupt again. We are coming close to the time when we -- and we have to be very strict at the end of the morning, since the courtroom will be used for another trial this afternoon, I think. If you would come, within a couple of minutes, to a point where you can stop the cross-examination, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to have the response to my question, that is, who was the other party involved in the fighting for Pofalici? He told us about one of the factions. I would like to know about the other.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the other side consisted of those who were attacking the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: Just the other side. There's no third side. There was no third side for the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But who were they? Who was this other side as regards the fighting for Pofalici? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA MULAOMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will break for now, in view of the time, and resume my cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, could you please give us an indication how much time you would still need? I have written down that if we would allow you the same time as the Prosecution for examination-in-chief, you would still have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will respect the time which was allocated to the Prosecution and which you have allocated to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of January, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
